title: Introduction to Window Functions
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Introduction to Window Functions.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to window function concepts.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Introduction to Window Functions. Its primary job is to help you turn rows into correct summaries and analytics while respecting grouping, NULLs, window ordering and frames. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing introduction to window functions teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: turn rows into correct summaries and analytics while respecting grouping, NULLs, window ordering and frames. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Introduction to Window Functions
content_blocks.expected_output: Returns each order with a per-customer sequence. Ties remain deterministic because id is included in ORDER BY.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Assumes orders(customer_id, order_date, total, id). Window ordering affects the calculation, not final output ordering.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Introduction to Window Functions”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Window function concepts”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Window function concepts”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Introduction to Window Functions, with an explanation of “Window function concepts”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Introduction to Window Functions fits into the broader goal to turn rows into correct summaries and analytics while respecting grouping, NULLs, window ordering and frames.
